Powers of ten use ^{...} run markup with the true minus U+2212 (Archivo carries it); the hand-built figures draw the same superscripts. Nothing PROVISIONAL is on a student slide; flag F1 is labeled in teacher notes. The optional Bohr-radius slide (brief slide 17) is not built. No learning-target slide: the 20-content-slide cap is full, so targets sit in slide 1 notes.

fields.headline: The Bohr Model
fields.subhead: Find hydrogen's energy levels, and explain emission and absorption as an electron changing level.

imageSubjects.section: a hydrogen gas discharge tube glowing pink-magenta on a dark bench, lit only by its own light

slides.notes: Targets: describe Bohr's hydrogen model; use E_n = −2.18 × 10^{−18} J ÷ n² for a level energy and ΔE; explain emission and absorption; state the model's limits. Hook is the next slide. PROVISIONAL (brief flag F1, Matt to confirm): E_n needs scientific notation, but the course sequencing rule delays scientific notation and heavy math. Plan used: a pre-built table plus ONE student calculation, 3 sig figs, no sig-fig rules taught. Image prompt (empty slot): a hydrogen gas discharge tube glowing pink-magenta on a dark bench, lit only by its own light.

fields.headline: Why Only a Few Colors?
fields.subhead: Heat hydrogen gas and it glows. A prism spreads that glow into a few thin lines of color, not a rainbow.
fields.keyq: Why does hydrogen give only a few colors of light?

imageSubjects.concept: a glowing hydrogen discharge tube photographed close, with a prism-split smear of four thin colored lines beside it

slides.notes: Pose the question and leave it open; it is answered by slide 20. Do not name quantization yet. Image prompt (empty slot): a glowing hydrogen discharge tube photographed close, with a prism-split smear of four thin colored lines beside it.

fields.headline: Three Words You Need First
fields.subhead: Write the first one down. The other two come back on later slides.
fields.k1_b:
One allowed energy for the electron.
Labeled n = 1, 2, 3, and up.
fields.k2_b:
Only certain values are allowed.
Nothing in between.
fields.k3_b:
A packet of light.
Its energy sets its color.
fields.mustwrite: Energy level: one allowed energy for the electron, labeled n.

imageSubjects.aside: a glass prism on a lab bench splitting a narrow white beam

slides.notes: Vocabulary first so later slides can use it. Students write only the energy-level line. Image prompt (empty slot): a glass prism on a lab bench splitting a narrow white beam.

fields.headline: Why Bohr Needed a New Model
fields.subhead: Rutherford put the electrons outside a dense nucleus. That left a problem.
fields.c1_b:
Thomson: electrons inside positive material.

Rutherford, 1911: a dense nucleus, electrons outside it.
fields.c2_b:
A charge moving in a circle should give off energy and spiral into the nucleus.

Atoms do not collapse.
fields.mustwrite: Bohr proposed a new model of the hydrogen atom in 1913.

imageSubjects.concept: a chalkboard with a hand-drawn nucleus and one looping electron path, chalk dust on the ledge

slides.notes: Thomson, then Rutherford 1911, then the problem: a classical orbiting charge should radiate and spiral in. Bohr, 1913. Image prompt (empty slot): a chalkboard with a hand-drawn nucleus and one looping electron path, chalk dust on the ledge.

fields.headline: Bohr's Three Ideas
fields.subhead: He kept the nucleus and put rules on the electron.
fields.k1_b:
The electron moves in a circular orbit.
Each orbit has one fixed energy.
fields.k2_b: In an allowed orbit, the electron does not give off energy.
fields.k3_b: It changes orbit only by absorbing or emitting a photon.
fields.mustwrite: The photon's energy equals the energy difference between the two orbits.

imageSubjects.aside: a hand-drawn set of concentric circles in a pocket notebook, pencil beside it

slides.notes: Three rules: fixed orbits, no radiation in an orbit, photon jumps. The photon energy equals the difference between the two levels. Image prompt (empty slot): a hand-drawn set of concentric circles in a pocket notebook, pencil beside it.

fields.headline: Bohr's Hydrogen Atom
fields.subhead: One proton, one electron, orbits at fixed distances.
fields.a1_b: One proton, drawn as the dot in the center.
fields.a2_b: n = 1, 2, 3 and up. Farther out is higher energy.
fields.a3_b: One electron, in one orbit at a time. Here: n = 1.

slides.notes: Diagram: one proton, one electron, here at n = 1. Orbit radii run 1 : 4 : 9. This is the model's picture, not reality; slide 19 returns to that.

fields.headline: Quantized Means Steps, Not a Ramp
fields.subhead: You can stand on a stair. You cannot stand between two stairs.
fields.c1_b:
Only certain heights.

An electron's energy works like this.
fields.c2_b:
Any height at all.

Electrons do not behave this way.
fields.mustwrite: Quantized: only certain energy values are allowed. Nothing in between.

imageSubjects.concept: a wooden staircase beside a smooth ramp of the same height, side-lit

slides.notes: Stairs versus ramp. Stress that no energy exists between levels. Image prompt (empty slot): a wooden staircase beside a smooth ramp of the same height, side-lit.

fields.headline: The Energy of Each Level
fields.subhead: Put in n and you get that level's energy, in joules.
fields.a2_b: The electron is bound to the nucleus. E = 0 is a free electron.
fields.a3_b: This formula fails for atoms with 2 or more electrons.

slides.notes: Equation: E_n = −2.18 × 10^{−18} J ÷ n². n is a whole number. Negative means bound; E = 0 is a free electron. Hydrogen only. PROVISIONAL (brief flag F1, Matt to confirm): E_n needs scientific notation, but the course sequencing rule delays scientific notation and heavy math. Plan used: a pre-built table plus ONE student calculation, 3 sig figs, no sig-fig rules taught.

fields.headline: Hydrogen's Energy Levels
fields.subhead: Drawn to scale. Watch what happens to the spacing.
fields.a1_b: More negative means lower. n = 1 is the lowest.
fields.a2_b: The levels crowd together as n gets larger.
fields.a3_b: n = ∞ is E = 0. The electron has left the atom.

slides.notes: Values to n = 6: n=1 −2.18 × 10^{−18} J; n=2 −5.45 × 10^{−19}; n=3 −2.42 × 10^{−19}; n=4 −1.36 × 10^{−19}; n=5 −8.72 × 10^{−20}; n=6 −6.06 × 10^{−20}. Spacing is drawn to scale. Misconception: more negative means more energy. It means lower. n = ∞ is E = 0.

fields.headline: Example: Energy at n = 3
fields.subhead: We do this one together. Write the setup, not just the number.
fields.problem: What is the energy of the hydrogen electron when n = 3?

imageSubjects.aside: a pencil resting beside a scientific calculator on a lab notebook

slides.notes: Worked together. Answer: 3² = 9; −2.18 × 10^{−18} ÷ 9 = −2.42 × 10^{−19} J. Students write the setup, not just the number. Image prompt (empty slot): a pencil resting beside a scientific calculator on a lab notebook.

fields.headline: n = 3, Worked
fields.subhead: Square n first, then divide.
fields.mustwrite: Less negative means higher energy. E₃ is above E₂.

slides.notes: Check against slide 9: −2.42 × 10^{−19} is less negative than E₂ = −5.45 × 10^{−19}, so E₃ is higher. Calculator use is fine; 3 sig figs, no sig-fig rules taught.

fields.headline: Ground State and Excited States
fields.subhead: Hydrogen's electron has one lowest level and many higher ones.
fields.c1_b:
n = 1.
The lowest energy level.

Where the electron normally sits.
fields.c2_b:
Any level above n = 1.

Short-lived. The electron falls back down.
fields.mustwrite: Ground state: n = 1. Excited state: any higher n.

imageSubjects.concept: two hydrogen discharge tubes side by side, one dark and one glowing

slides.notes: Ground state is n = 1. Excited states are any higher n and are short-lived. Image prompt (empty slot): two hydrogen discharge tubes side by side, one dark and one glowing.

fields.headline: Absorption: The Electron Goes Up
fields.subhead: The atom takes in energy from a photon.
fields.a1_b: Photon energy must equal E final minus E initial.
fields.a2_b: The photon passes through. Nothing happens.
fields.a3_b: The electron moves up. The atom gains energy.

slides.notes: Absorption: the electron rises only if the photon energy equals exactly E final minus E initial. Wrong-energy photons pass through. Misconception: that any photon will do.

fields.headline: Emission: The Electron Drops
fields.subhead: The atom gives energy out as a photon.
fields.a1_b: The electron falls from a higher level to a lower one.
fields.a2_b: Its energy is the absolute value of ΔE.
fields.a3_b: A bigger drop gives a higher-energy photon.

slides.notes: Emission: the electron drops and a photon leaves with energy |ΔE|. A bigger drop is a higher-energy photon. Misconception: emission means the electron goes up. It drops. Colors and wavelengths are S2.5, not here.

fields.headline: Example: Drop from n = 3 to n = 2
fields.subhead: Find the energy change, then say where the energy went.
fields.problem: A hydrogen electron drops from n = 3 to n = 2. Find ΔE. Is energy absorbed or released?
fields.mustwrite: ΔE = final energy minus initial energy. A negative ΔE means energy leaves the atom.

imageSubjects.aside: a camera-flash bulb mid-discharge in a dark room

slides.notes: Worked together. Answer: ΔE = E₂ − E₃ = −5.45 × 10^{−19} − (−2.42 × 10^{−19}) = −3.03 × 10^{−19} J. Negative, so energy is released. Image prompt (empty slot): a camera-flash bulb mid-discharge in a dark room.

fields.headline: n = 3 to n = 2, Worked
fields.subhead: Final minus initial. Keep the negative signs.
fields.f1_b:
ΔE = E₂ − E₃
Final level: n = 2
Initial level: n = 3
fields.mustwrite: Energy released: a photon of 3.03 × 10^{−19} J leaves the atom.

slides.notes: Final minus initial, keep the negatives. Photon energy is 3.03 × 10^{−19} J. Do not calculate its wavelength; that is S2.5.

fields.headline: Example: Removing the Electron
fields.subhead: Ionization means n goes all the way to infinity.
fields.problem: How much energy removes the electron from a hydrogen atom in its ground state?
fields.g1_b:
Hydrogen, ground state
n = 1 to n = ∞
E at n = ∞ is 0
fields.mustwrite: Ionization: the electron goes from its level to n = ∞, where E = 0.

imageSubjects.aside: a spark gap between two electrodes in a dark lab

slides.notes: Worked together. Answer: n = 1 to ∞, ΔE = 0 − (−2.18 × 10^{−18}) = +2.18 × 10^{−18} J, absorbed. Image prompt (empty slot): a spark gap between two electrodes in a dark lab.

fields.headline: Ionization, Worked
fields.subhead: Final minus initial again. The sign tells you the direction.
fields.f1_b:
ΔE = final − initial
Final (n = ∞): 0
Initial (n = 1): E₁
fields.mustwrite: A positive ΔE means energy absorbed. Ionizing hydrogen takes 2.18 × 10^{−18} J.

slides.notes: Positive ΔE means absorbed. Ionization energy of ground-state hydrogen is 2.18 × 10^{−18} J.

fields.headline: Where the Bohr Model Stops Working
fields.subhead: It was a real step forward. It is no longer the accepted model.
fields.k1_b: Correct energies for hydrogen. Wrong for He, Li, and every atom with 2 or more electrons.
fields.k2_b: Electrons are not particles on circular tracks. The electron-cloud model replaces the orbits.
fields.k3_b:
Quantized energy levels.
A level change means a photon in or out.
fields.mustwrite: Keep this: energy is quantized, and a change of level means a photon in or out.

imageSubjects.aside: a worn textbook diagram of concentric orbits with a pencil strike through it

slides.notes: Limits: correct for hydrogen only, not for atoms with 2 or more electrons. Electrons are not particles on tracks; the electron-cloud model (S2.2) replaces the orbits. Keep: quantized levels, photon in or out. Image prompt (empty slot): a worn textbook diagram of concentric orbits with a pencil strike through it.

fields.headline: Quick Check: Items 1 to 3
fields.subhead: Work these on your own paper, then we compare.
fields.k1_b: Explain why hydrogen emits light at only certain colors. Use the word quantized.
fields.k2_b: Calculate the energy of the hydrogen electron at n = 2.
fields.k3_b: A hydrogen electron drops from n = 4 to n = 2. Is energy absorbed or released? How much?
fields.mustwrite: For every calculation, write the equation first, then the numbers, then the units.

imageSubjects.aside: a student's notebook page with a calculation crossed out and redone

slides.notes: Check answers. 1: Electron energy is quantized, so only certain level differences exist and only certain photon energies, hence certain colors. 2: E₂ = −2.18 × 10^{−18} ÷ 4 = −5.45 × 10^{−19} J. 3: Emitted. E₄ = −1.36 × 10^{−19}, E₂ = −5.45 × 10^{−19}, ΔE = −4.09 × 10^{−19} J, so 4.09 × 10^{−19} J leaves the atom. Image prompt (empty slot): a student's notebook page with a calculation crossed out and redone.

fields.headline: Quick Check: Items 4 and 5
fields.subhead: Same as before. Your own paper first.
fields.c1_b: Which drop releases more energy, n = 3 to n = 2 or n = 2 to n = 1? Find both ΔE values.
fields.c2_b: Give one reason the Bohr model is no longer the accepted model of the atom.
fields.mustwrite: ΔE = final energy minus initial energy.

imageSubjects.concept: a stack of graded quiz papers with a red pen on top

slides.notes: Check answers. 4: n = 2 to 1 releases more. ΔE(3→2) = −3.03 × 10^{−19} J; ΔE(2→1) = −2.18 × 10^{−18} − (−5.45 × 10^{−19}) = −1.64 × 10^{−18} J. 5: any one of: works only for hydrogen; cannot predict multi-electron atoms; electrons are not particles in circular orbits. Image prompt (empty slot): a stack of graded quiz papers with a red pen on top.
